site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: The Monkey's Quick Heart
stories.source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
body: By a river in India, a monkey lived in a fruit tree, and each day he tossed the sweetest mangoes down to a crocodile who floated below. Their friendship seemed gentle and true, until the crocodile's wife grew jealous and demanded the monkey's heart for her dinner.

The crocodile invited the monkey to cross the water on his back, then confessed his wicked errand halfway across. But the monkey was quicker, crying that his heart still hung among the branches of the tree and he must fetch it. Believing the lie, the crocodile turned the boat of his back around.

At the bank the monkey sprang into the leaves, safe and laughing, and watched the crocodile drift away, defeated by his own greed. The river ran on, the mangoes ripened, and the monkey had learned at last to read the warning in a friend's eyes.

stories.title: Milk from Lalo's Bread
stories.source: Janamsakhi tradition; M. A. Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, vol. I (1909, public domain)
body: Guru Nanak chose to stay with Bhai Lalo, a poor carpenter who earned his bread by honest labor, instead of accepting the grand feast prepared by the wealthy official Malik Bhago. Lalo offered what little he had with open hands and a humble heart.

When Bhago came, offended and demanding an answer, Nanak pressed Lalo's coarse bread in one hand and a dish from the lavish banquet in the other. From Lalo's bread, pure milk flowed, while from Bhago's rich food, blood seeped forth, revealing the quiet truth of how each man's living was earned.

Bhago understood the gentle rebuke and bowed his head. He changed his ways, honoring the dignity of honest work. In that small home, the humble laborer's bread was blessed, and the world tilted, just a little, toward grace.

stories.title: Shelter Beneath Govardhana
body: When Indra's storm clouds thundered over Vrindavana and the rain fell without mercy, the cowherds and their cattle trembled before the flooding sky. Young Krishna, seeing their fear, walked calmly to the great Govardhana Hill and lifted it aloft with a single hand.

He held the mountain like a vast green umbrella, and beneath its shelter the families of Vrindavana huddled safely with their cows for seven days and seven nights. The wind howled above, but warmth and quiet held them below as Krishna bore the weight without wearying.

At last Indra discerned the divine strength upholding the hill, and he withdrew his storms in humility, seeking Krishna's forgiveness. Gently Krishna lowered Govardhana back to its place, and the village rejoiced in peace, unity, and gratitude.

stories.title: The Yaksha's Gentle Blessing
body: Deep in the forest beside a quiet lake, Yudhishthira found his brothers lying still, struck down because they had ignored the Yaksha's hidden questions. The wise brother, instead of rushing forward, knelt and listened carefully to every word the unseen guardian spoke.

When the Yaksha offered him the life of a single brother, Yudhishthira chose Nakula, saying his mother Madri must have a son as well as Kunti. This answer, so steady and fair, pleased the guardian of the lake beyond measure.

Touched by such dharmic grace, the Yaksha let the waters flow again and lifted every brother whole and breathing. Blessing the five Pandavas, he sent them onward with renewed strength and a gentler hope warming their journey home.

stories.title: Two Caravans in the Desert
stories.source: Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1912), Project Gutenberg
body: Two merchants set out across the dry desert with their caravans, wares piled high on wooden carts. The foolish one, easily swayed by passing strangers, was told that recent rain had filled the pools ahead, so he poured out his water skins and pressed onward with renewed hope.

The wise merchant studied those strangers carefully and noticed their wagon wheels were dry and their clothes carried no trace of mud or wet wind. Trusting his own eyes, he kept every waterskin and steered his people safely toward the spring he knew still waited.

Along the path he came upon the foolish merchant's abandoned caravan, and gathering what goods could still be saved, he carried them gently along. His alertness had protected his own people and turned another's loss into a quiet act of rescue.
